task: My best friend since fourth grade, Marcus, is moving to Portland next Monday and I want to send him a goodbye text that's heartfelt but also a little funny. Something about the time we got lost in Yellowstone and how I'm going to miss him, and that he owes me a visit.
rewrite:
ambition: A top pro (a speechwriter who does best-man toasts) would build the whole text on one shared memory and let the joke carry the sincere line. They'd put the laugh first and the feeling last, and they wouldn't use greeting-card phrases like "you'll always be in my heart."

agency: The rawest material is your own memory of the Yellowstone trip: where you got lost, what Marcus said, what went wrong. It also includes how the two of you really text each other. None of that is in reach here, so the text assumes only that you got lost in Yellowstone and invents no further details.

acceleration: Use a callback. Make "getting lost in Yellowstone" the running joke, then flip it into the sincere point: being lost with Marcus was still the best part, and Portland is just a longer detour. Use a short, casual text rhythm, and close on the visit he owes you so the last line is both funny and an invitation.

accuracy: Nothing outside you can check a text like this. The closest proxy is a read-aloud test: it should sound like you texting Marcus and not like a card. Marcus's reply is the real test, and you can judge it before sending.

deeper task:
Write a goodbye text from me to Marcus, my best friend since fourth grade, who moves to Portland next Monday. It should be heartfelt with a little humor. Build it around the time we got lost in Yellowstone: use that as the joke, then turn it into the sincere point that I'll miss him. End by reminding him he owes me a visit. Make it sound like a real text between lifelong friends: casual, a few lines long, no greeting-card phrasing, and no invented details about the trip beyond us getting lost.

answers.plain:
Here's a draft you can tweak:

---

Marcus, I can't believe you're really leaving Monday. Twenty-some years of friendship, and you're ditching me for a city with more rain and better coffee.

I keep thinking about Yellowstone. Us, hopelessly lost, you insisting you knew a shortcut, me pretending to believe you. Somehow that's still one of my favorite days ever. If I'm going to be lost with anyone, it's you.

I'm going to miss you like crazy. Who else is going to laugh at my terrible jokes and tell me when I'm being an idiot?

Go crush it in Portland. But you owe me a visit, and this time I'm navigating.

Love you, man. 🧡

---

A few notes for making it yours:

- **Details:** If you remember specifics from the Yellowstone trip (a wrong turn, a bear scare, a snack crisis), swap one in. A real detail will land better than my generic one.
- **Years:** I guessed "twenty-some" from fourth grade. Change it to the actual number if you want.
- **Tone:** If you want it funnier, add a line like "Don't forget, you still owe me for the gas on that trip." If you want it more sentimental, cut the coffee joke.

Want a shorter version, or one that leans more into the humor?
answers.nudge:
Here's a main version, plus a shorter one and a few tips.

**Main version**

> Marcus. Portland. Next Monday. I'm trying to be mature about this and I'm failing.
>
> We've been best friends since fourth grade, so I don't really know how to do this without you down the street. You've been there for basically every version of me, including the one who thought it was a good idea to navigate Yellowstone with [a paper map / "a great sense of direction"]. We were lost for hours and I still wouldn't trade it. Honestly, getting lost with you is the best way to see a place.
>
> I'm so proud of you, and I'm going to miss you like crazy. But I want it on record that you owe me a visit. I'm expecting a guest room, good coffee, and a tour from someone who actually knows where they're going this time. (Okay, maybe I'll drive. Neither of us should be trusted with directions.)
>
> Love you, man. Call me when you land.

**Shorter version**

> Marcus, I can't believe you're really leaving. Fourth grade to Portland, what a run. I'll miss you more than I'll admit, and I'll never forget us lost in Yellowstone, which is still the best bad day of my life. You owe me a visit. Don't make me come find you without a map. Love you, brother.

**Making it yours**

- **Fill in the Yellowstone detail.** The text lands best with one specific, true moment, like who insisted they knew the way, what you ate, or the line he kept repeating. A real detail is funnier and more touching than anything I can invent. Replace my bracketed guess with it.
- **Match how you two talk.** If you usually trade insults, make the teasing sharper. If you're more sincere, cut the jokes down to one.
- **Keep the order.** Start with a laugh, put the heartfelt part in the middle, and end on the visit. The ask then reads as a promise to see each other again, not a sad goodbye.
- **Consider saying it in person too.** Send this now, then take him to dinner or a last drive before Monday.

If you tell me what actually happened in Yellowstone, I'll rewrite the text around it.
answers.skill:
Here's a draft:

> Marcus, I've been trying to figure out how to say this without getting weird, so I'm just gonna say it. Portland is lucky, but I'm not happy about it.
>
> Fourth grade to now, and the best proof of our friendship is that we got lost in Yellowstone and I still would've picked you to be lost with. Anyone else and I'd have been furious. With you it was kind of the best part.
>
> Anyway, I'm going to miss you a lot. Not having you 10 minutes away is going to suck.
>
> You owe me a visit. Don't make me come find you. We both know how that goes.

A couple of notes: I assumed you two live fairly close, so tweak the "10 minutes away" line if that's not right. I also kept it to the lost-in-Yellowstone detail only, as you asked. If you'd like it shorter or goofier, I can trim it.
